0.1.title: How we know anything: the sources
0.1.prompt: Give me an in-depth report on the sources for Roman history and mythology, with the emphasis on the problem that defines the subject: Rome's early history was written down centuries after the events, by Romans with agendas. Cover: the first Roman historians, who wrote in Greek (Fabius Pictor, writing around 200 BC; Cincius Alimentus) and why they did; Cato's Origines and the Latin annalists (Cassius Hemina, Calpurnius Piso, Valerius Antias, Claudius Quadrigarius, Licinius Macer), known only in fragments, and the charge that they invented; the raw material they claimed to use (the Annales Maximi of the pontiffs, the lists of consuls and triumphs, family archives, funeral orations) and the complaints Cicero and Livy themselves make about it; the surviving narratives: Polybius (the outsider's analysis), Livy (Ab urbe condita, 142 books of which 35 survive, and his preface on legend), Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Roman Antiquities, and his thesis that Rome was a Greek city), Diodorus, Plutarch's Roman Lives, Appian and Cassius Dio for the later Republic; the antiquarians (Varro, Verrius Flaccus through Festus, Aulus Gellius, Macrobius) for religion and custom; and the imperial historians in outline (Velleius, Tacitus, Suetonius, the Historia Augusta, Ammianus). Material sources: inscriptions (the Lapis Niger, the Duenos vase, the Satricum stone, the Scipio epitaphs, the Res Gestae, Claudius' speech on the Lyon tablet), coins as propaganda, the Pyrgi tablets, and archaeology in the Forum and on the Palatine. Then the method: the hypercritical tradition from Niebuhr and Mommsen to Pais and Forsythe, the more trusting positions of Cornell and Carandini, Wiseman's view of the early stories as dramatic inventions, and how to judge a story first found in Livy. End with the main traps: treating Livy book 1 as history, treating Dionysius as independent of Livy, trusting the Historia Augusta, and reading Roman myth only through Ovid. Point back to Greek module 0.1 for the Greek sources rather than repeating them. Format: about 3000 words, headed sections, name sources, flag disagreements, end with a 10-question self-test with answers and the three ideas I must carry forward.
